questions.title: Testing two guide RNAs
questions.stem:
Researchers target a bacterial reporter gene with Cas9 and guide A or B. A control receives Cas9 without a targeting guide. Equal numbers of colonies are sampled after treatment. A sequencing test detects the intended edit and a separate test detects an edit at one predicted off-target locus. The two counts can overlap.

| Treatment | Colonies tested | Intended edit | Off-target edit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | 200 | 2 | 1 |
| Guide A | 200 | 156 | 18 |
| Guide B | 200 | 124 | 4 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the intended-edit percentage and off-target percentage for each guide.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For guide A, calculate the possible range of colonies with both the intended edit and no detected off-target edit. Explain why one exact value cannot be found.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the roles of complementarity and Cas9 in the targeting mechanism, and why an imperfect off-target match could be relevant.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Assess the claim that B is the safer guide for all purposes and propose a stronger test.

steps.text: A intended=156/200×100=78% and B intended=62%.
A off-target=9% and B off-target=2%.
A gives the greater intended percentage but B the lower measured off-target percentage.
At most all 156 intended edits are in colonies without the off-target edit.
At least 156−18=138 intended-edited colonies lack that off-target edit.
The overlap between the two positive groups was not recorded, so 138–156 are possible.
The guide RNA base-pairs with a complementary target DNA sequence.
Cas9 recognizes an appropriate adjacent motif and cuts the target DNA.
A sufficiently similar second site can also be bound and cut, giving undesired sequence changes after repair.
B has a lower detected off-target frequency at the one assayed locus in the surviving colonies.
Other sites or effects on survival are not represented, so a universal safety claim is unsupported.
Sequence additional off-target sites or genomes and measure survival with independent treated cultures and matched controls.

questions.title: Following labelled carbon in an alga
questions.stem:
A ¹⁴CO₂ pulse is delivered to an illuminated culture and then replaced by unlabelled CO₂. The table reports the percentage of all recovered label in three fractions. Recoveries are normalized separately at each time.

| Time after pulse / s | 3-carbon acids / % | Sugar phosphates / % | Other products / % |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 76 | 16 | 8 |
| 10 | 38 | 43 | 19 |
| 40 | 12 | 49 | 39 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Quantify the change in the share of label in 3-carbon acids between 2 s and 40 s in two ways.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why early label in 3-carbon acids is consistent with the first fixation step of the Calvin cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how light-dependent products enable some of this carbon to reach carbohydrate while fixation continues.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why the percentages do not prove that every labelled atom passed directly from the first listed fraction to the second, and suggest an improvement.

steps.text: The share decreases by 76−12=64 percentage points.
Its relative decrease is 64/76×100≈84%.
These are changes in shares of recovered label, not absolute quantities of compound.
Rubisco catalyses addition of CO₂ to RuBP.
The unstable six-carbon intermediate splits.
This yields two three-carbon phosphoglycerate molecules, one initially carrying the newly fixed carbon.
ATP supplies energy and reduced NADP supplies reducing power in conversion to triose phosphate.
Some triose phosphate can be used to synthesize carbohydrates.
The rest contributes to regeneration of RuBP using ATP, allowing continued fixation.
The data combine many molecules and alternative routes may contribute.
Each time point is normalized separately, masking total recovered radioactivity.
Resolve individual intermediates at more closely spaced times and measure absolute label recovery; accept another tracking design.

questions.title: Pressure differences and blood flow
questions.stem:
A model systemic circulation has flow F=(arterial pressure−venous pressure)/resistance. Pressures are in kPa. Values below are means over a cardiac cycle. Resting cardiac output is 5.0 dm³ min⁻¹.

| Condition | Mean arterial pressure | Mean venous pressure | Relative systemic resistance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rest | 13.0 | 1.0 | 1.00 |
| Exercise | 15.0 | 1.5 | 0.75 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the pressure difference at rest and exercise and find the predicted exercise-to-rest flow ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate predicted exercise output and stroke volume if exercise heart rate is 125 min⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how arterioles in active muscle can contribute to a lower vascular resistance and altered distribution of flow.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Why would mean pressures be inadequate to determine the instant the aortic valve opens? State the necessary comparison and the consequence of valve closure.

steps.text: Differences are 12.0 and 13.5 kPa.
Predicted flow ratio is 1.50.
Exercise output=5.0×1.50=7.5 dm³ min⁻¹.
Stroke volume=7.5/125=0.060 dm³ beat⁻¹.
This is 60 cm³ beat⁻¹ with the correct volume conversion.
Smooth muscle relaxation increases the arteriolar lumen diameter.
At a given pressure difference the wider lumen reduces resistance and increases local flow.
If vessels in other beds dilate less or constrict, a larger fraction of cardiac output reaches active muscle.
A mean hides within-cycle changes in pressure.
Opening occurs when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, requiring simultaneous time-resolved measurements.
Closure prevents backflow into the ventricle when aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure.

questions.title: Following viral replication
questions.stem:
A bacterial culture receives bacteriophages at time zero. After a short adsorption period the cells are washed. At each time, researchers assay free infective particles in a filtered sample. The experiment starts with 2.0×10⁵ infected bacteria per cm³. Assume one lytic cycle and negligible decay.

| Time / min | 5 | 15 | 25 | 35 | 45 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free infective particles / cm³ | 10000 | 10000 | 20000 | 11000000 | 12010000 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the burst size from the final increase above residual free particles. State the necessary assumption about infected bacteria.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why a low early free-particle count does not mean viral nucleic acid is absent.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish lytic replication from a lysogenic association using the fate of the host and viral genome.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest how to test whether a resistant surviving bacterial colony carries a prophage and evaluate a positive DNA result.

steps.text: Increase=12010000−10000=12000000 particles cm⁻³.
Estimated burst=12000000/(2.0×10⁵)=60 particles per infected bacterium.
Assumes each counted infected cell completes the cycle and releases progeny once.
Viral genomes can be inside infected host cells.
The assay samples free infective particles after removal of cells.
Assembly and release can lag behind intracellular genome replication.
In a lytic cycle viral genome and proteins are produced and progeny assembled.
Lysis releases particles and kills the host cell.
In lysogeny a prophage is maintained and copied with the host genome without immediate lysis.
Test colony DNA for a phage–host integration junction using suitable primers or sequencing.
Use known lysogenic positive and phage-free negative controls.
A junction supports integration but does not alone establish production of viable phage; induce and assay particles to test that.

questions.title: From enzyme shape to metabolic control
questions.stem: A cell regulates a branched pathway. A product inhibits an enzyme near the beginning of its own branch.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline the role of activation energy and how an enzyme changes reaction rate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how an enzyme–substrate interaction can generate specificity and catalysis.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain feedback inhibition and how a student could distinguish reversible competitive inhibition from a reduction in maximum catalytic capacity.

parts.label: quality
parts.prompt: Quality of the complete extended response

steps.text: Reactants must reach a transition state requiring activation energy.
The enzyme provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation barrier.
At a given temperature more collisions can result in reaction per unit time.
The active site has a particular three-dimensional arrangement of side chains.
Shape and chemical properties favour binding of suitable substrates.
Binding can induce a conformational change that improves interactions.
The enzyme can orient substrates or stabilize the transition state, facilitating bond changes.
Products leave and the enzyme can catalyse another cycle.
A downstream product binds a regulatory site on an earlier enzyme.
A conformational change reduces that enzyme's activity.
As product accumulates, flux through the pathway falls, conserving substrates or energy.
When product level falls, inhibition is relieved and flux can rise again.
Measure initial rates across a range of substrate concentrations with and without inhibitor while controlling enzyme concentration and temperature.
Under simple reversible competitive inhibition, sufficiently high substrate can approach the same maximum rate.
A persistent lower plateau at saturating substrate supports reduced catalytic capacity; the pattern alone need not identify the exact binding site.

Award one mark when the complete response communicates the relevant biological reasoning clearly and concisely, with logical connections and little repetition. Assess this across the parts, independently of the content score.

questions.title: Water movement from soil to air
questions.stem: A terrestrial plant has access to moist soil while its leaves are exposed to dry air. Consider water potential and transport through the plant.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Distinguish solute potential from pressure potential and relate them to total water potential in a cell.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain water uptake from soil into a root and onward delivery to xylem when the gradient is favourable.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the cohesion–tension mechanism and how a prolonged drought can limit carbon gain.

parts.label: quality
parts.prompt: Quality of the complete extended response

steps.text: Dissolved solutes lower water potential relative to pure water, giving a negative solute potential.
Pressure exerted on cell contents by the wall usually provides a positive pressure potential in a turgid cell.
Ignoring gravity and other components, total water potential is the sum of solute and pressure potentials.
Root hairs increase contact area with soil solution.
Solute accumulation can lower root-cell water potential.
Water moves across a partially permeable membrane by osmosis down the water-potential gradient.
Water can move across cortex through walls or through cell contents.
Selective passage through endodermal cells regulates entry of solutes into the vascular tissue; accept an accurate explanation of the Casparian strip.
Water evaporates from moist internal leaf surfaces.
Water vapour diffuses out through stomata down its gradient.
Loss of water generates tension in the leaf xylem.
Cohesion maintains continuity of water columns as tension is transmitted down the xylem.
Water is pulled upward to replace water lost at leaves.
Under water deficit, stomata can close, reducing transpiration.
Closure restricts CO₂ entry and can lower photosynthetic carbon fixation.

Award one mark when the complete response communicates the relevant biological reasoning clearly and concisely, with logical connections and little repetition. Assess this across the parts, independently of the content score.

questions.title: Chromosomes, linkage and variation
questions.stem: A diploid organism is heterozygous at two loci on the same chromosome. Its gametes show two common and two less common allele combinations.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline how homologous chromosomes differ from sister chromatids.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the events in meiosis that allow gametes to receive one allele at each locus and different combinations at linked loci.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discuss how test-cross progeny can be used to infer linkage, with limits on the inference.

parts.label: quality
parts.prompt: Quality of the complete extended response

steps.text: Homologues carry corresponding loci and one member comes from each parent.
They may have different alleles at a locus.
Sister chromatids arise by replication of one chromosome and initially carry matching DNA sequences, apart from copying errors.
DNA replicates once before meiosis begins.
Homologous chromosomes pair in prophase I.
Crossing over between non-sister chromatids can exchange segments between the loci.
Homologues separate in the first meiotic division, reducing chromosome number.
Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, generating haploid products.
Cross the double heterozygote with an individual recessive at both loci.
Provided phenotypes reliably reveal genotype, each offspring identifies the heterozygote's gamete type.
Independent assortment with equal transmission and survival predicts four equally frequent classes.
An excess of the two parental classes supports linkage.
Recombinant percentage equals the combined nonparental counts divided by total progeny times 100.
Double crossovers can restore a parental marker arrangement and cause underestimation of physical separation.
Differential viability or small samples can distort observed frequencies; use sufficient progeny and test goodness of fit or score earlier stages.

Award one mark when the complete response communicates the relevant biological reasoning clearly and concisely, with logical connections and little repetition. Assess this across the parts, independently of the content score.
